title: How Perfume Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how perfume works and its history. They open with banter about colognes (Drekar Noir, Benetton Colors) and whether scents go bad. They trace perfume's origins from priests burning incense to cover animal sacrifice odors, to the use of animal scent glands and ambergris, and to Grasse, France, where scented leather gloves gained fame after Catherine de Medici. They explain perfume composition: perfume oil diluted in alcohol and water, the forms of perfume by concentration, and top, heart, and base notes that evaporate in sequence. They cover Channel No. 5 and Marilyn Monroe, odor categories, how fragrance houses create a perfume from a client brief (using chemists, perfumers, gas chromatography, and headspace), and the Joop-style launch example. They also discuss the psychology of smell: why people wear perfume, whether smell preference is learned (winter green example) or innate, the Army's failed stink bomb, and claims about pheromones and attraction. The episode closes with a listener mail about Nostradamus and the end-of-the-world prediction.

segments.title: Opening banter and cologne talk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke around, discussing Drakkar Noir and Benetton Colors and whether colognes go bad when stored improperly.

segments.title: Origins of perfume
segments.summary: Perfume's roots lie in priests burning incense to mask the smell of animal sacrifices. Ancient Egyptians then used animal scent glands on their bodies, and the purpose has stayed largely sexual since.

segments.title: Animal-derived scents: musk, castoreum, civet, ambergris
segments.summary: Early perfume ingredients came from animal scent glands, including musk deer, beaver castoreum, civet, and ambergris from sperm whales, which forms from material in the whale's gut and floats on the ocean. The hosts note ambergris is illegal in US perfumes.

segments.title: Chuck's dislike of synthetic scents and natural versus synthetic perfume
segments.summary: Chuck explains he dislikes perfumed products, such as scented sprays, detergents, and fabric softener. The hosts discuss that most perfumed products are synthetic and that essential oils are expensive.

segments.title: Grasse and the perfumed leather gloves of Catherine de Medici
segments.summary: Grasse in southern France became the perfume center because of its climate, which grows jasmine, orange blossom, and lavender. Its tanners perfumed stinky leather gloves and sent a pair to Catherine de Medici, who loved them, making Grasse the perfume capital.

segments.title: What perfume is: concentration and dilution
segments.summary: Perfume is mostly alcohol and water with odorant molecules. Perfume oil, parfum, eau de toilette (about ten percent), and eau de cologne (lighter) differ by how much solvent they contain. Cologne can also mean a men's scent.

segments.title: Channel No. 5, cologne trends, and perfume categories
segments.summary: Channel No. 5, the first perfume to use synthetic ingredients, became popular after Marilyn Monroe said she wore it. Cologne was popular, then fell away, then returned. The hosts list perfume families such as floral, fruity, green, woody, oriental, animalic, and fecal notes.

segments.title: Top, heart, and base notes and evaporation
segments.summary: Alcohol lets the different odor molecules evaporate in sequence. Top notes come first and fade within minutes, heart notes follow for up to an hour, and base notes last longest. The hosts compare this to a symphony and note that body chemistry changes how a scent smells.

segments.title: Applying perfume and pulse points
segments.summary: The hosts advise dabbing perfume on pulse points like the wrists and behind the ears, avoiding rubbing, which generates heat and breaks down top notes. Josh describes his walk-through method.

segments.title: How fragrance houses create a perfume
segments.summary: A company such as Polo writes a brief. Chemists and perfumers at fragrance houses produce dozens of formulas, use gas chromatography and headspace analysis to copy natural scents, and go through testing before a winner is chosen. Polo then produces and dilutes the perfume oil. Knockoff perfumes are legal if the formula is slightly tweaked.

segments.title: Why people wear perfume and learned versus innate smell
segments.summary: Rachel Herz's research on why people wear perfume by age and gender is discussed. The hosts cover the associative learning hypothesis, with the winter green example, versus the innate evolutionary view. They note the Army's failed universal stink bomb.

segments.title: Pheromones, attraction, and scent and immunity
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea that scent influences mate selection through immune system differences, and argue that cologne may deceive that signal. They say there is no scientific proof of a human aphrodisiac, and that pigs have a vomeronasal organ for pheromones which humans lack.

segments.title: Giorgio ban and closing remarks
segments.summary: Giorgio was banned from some restaurants because of its strength, which boosted sales. Chuck mentions the Obsession smell in his building's elevator.

segments.title: Listener mail: Nostradamus and the Gangnam Style prediction
segments.summary: A listener from Toronto, Julia Ka, writes about a supposed Nostradamus prediction linked to Gangnam Style and December 21 that the hosts read.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to share favorite or hated perfumes on social media and email, and direct them to the website.
